claims.text: Reasons that can justify a separate service include scaling one part on its own, releasing it on its own schedule, keeping its failures (crashes, slowness) away from the rest, or letting another team own it; without such a need, a module stays in the process.
At stage-2 deploy/k8s/api.yaml defines Deployment api in namespace donhang with replicas: 2 (line 11) and one container api from image ghcr.io/duyan11110/donhang-api:1.0.0.

A Deployment's spec.replicas sets how many Pods are created from its Pod template; every Pod runs the same containers, and the api container runs the app as one process (ENTRYPOINT dotnet DonHang.Api.dll), so a different count for the sender needs a different process under a different Deployment.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Concepts > Workloads > Deployments (replicas, Pod template); examples/don-hang @ stage-2: DonHang.Api/Dockerfile (ENTRYPOINT)

claims.text: At stage-2 NotificationQueue.ClaimDueAsync claims rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a transaction, so a row one api copy has locked is skipped by the other: two copies never claim the same row at the same time, and share the due emails between them.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL docs: SELECT > The Locking Clause (SKIP LOCKED); examples/don-hang @ stage-2: DonHang.Infrastructure/NotificationQueue.cs:16-30

claims.text: Sharing the API's count costs something only if the job needs a different number of copies than the API; while it does not, it is no reason to extract, and the second sender is not waste: its extra cost is a second copy of the loop.

A separate service brings costs: method calls become network calls that can be slow or fail, data saved in one transaction becomes separate saves, and one more image, pipeline and dashboard must be run.
claims.source_hint: design judgement; outline item 4; prereq design.l3.before-extracting-a-module claims 2, 6

claims.text: A modular monolith keeps the choice open: a module with a clean boundary can be extracted later when a reason appears, and its known ties let the team estimate the cost; not extracting now leaves extraction open, as long as the boundary stays clean.
Extracting is a decision with trade-offs, so writing down the options considered and why one was chosen (e.g. in a design doc) is part of making it.

One service per module as soon as possible is a mistake when there is no need; opposing view: when several teams already own separate modules and must each release on their own schedule, more services can be right.

Extraction does not always make a system faster: each call across the new boundary adds a network trip and a chance of failure; it can make the rest faster only when the moved part was competing with it for the same process's CPU and memory.
